snippet.title: The Great Australian Psychic Prediction Project (Rob Palmer)
snippet.description:
In 2021, "The Skeptic Zone" producer and CSI Fellow Richard Saunders completed his 12-year project dubbed the Great Australian Psychic Prediction Project (GAPPP) – an analysis of almost 4,000 published paranormal predictions made by over 200 people claiming paranormal powers in Australia. 

The scoring of the predictions was performed by an international team of volunteers of which Rob Palmer was a member. In this presentation, an expanded version of the talk given at CSICon 2022, Rob will share details and the results of this unique investigation into the precision (or lack thereof) of the published predictions of prominent, public, paranormal practitioners.

Rob Palmer is a retired aerospace engineer. He has been a spacecraft designer, spacecraft tester, computer programmer, and software systems engineer. Rob became a skeptical activist in 2016 upon joining the Guerrilla Skeptics on Wikipedia team, and in 2018 became a columnist for "Skeptical Inquirer." To date he has had over 70 articles published by "Skeptical Inquirer" as well as in other publications, and the Wikipedia articles he’s written have garnered over 13 million pageviews.

Rob writes about contemporary skeptical issues and has interviewed individuals as diverse as scientists Neil deGrasse Tyson, Richard Dawkins, and Robert Bartholomew, Penn Jillette, Ann Druyan (producer and writer for the modern Cosmos series), Seth Andrews (host of "The Thinking Atheist" podcast), and John de Lancie (Star Trek’s Q).

Rob is registered with the Center for Inquiry’s Speakers Bureau and has given presentations for various skeptic and humanist groups and conventions, including: We Can Reason, Dragon Con, and three times at CSICon (the annual science and skepticism conference in Las Vegas). His topics have included: Critical Thinking, the Wikipedia editing project he volunteers for (GSoW), the harm in believing in psychics and mediums, and the Great Australian Psychic Prediction Project. He has been interviewed about these subjects on various podcasts and YouTube shows, including "The Skeptic Zone," "Big Picture Science", "Be Rationable," "The Phil Ferguson Show", "Banachek’s Brain,"" 502 Conversations," Recovering from Religion, Point of Inquiry, and "The Thinking Atheist."

All of Rob’s skeptical work can be found at: https://linktr.ee/thewellknownskeptic.

snippet.description:
If Europe's "last pagans" sparked your curiosity, join other curious learners for an 8-week seminar exploring modern Pagan traditions with scholar Thorn Mooney: https://www.religiondepartment.com/contemporarypaganism

Europe was supposedly Christian by the Middle Ages, but the reality is more complicated. From the Sámi in Fennoscandia to the Baltic countryside, sacred groves, sacrifices, and animist traditions survived into the modern era.

snippet.title: Inside the Science of Weather and Climate Forecasting (Tom Di Liberto)
snippet.description:
Ever been stuck in a thunderstorm annoyed because your weather app says it was supposed to be sunny? Or saddled with three new unused shovels after reading a prediction for a snowier than normal winter? We've all been there, cursing the meteorologist. But what if I told you that 5-day weather forecasts can accurately predict the weather about 90% of the time. And that you're probably thinking about seasonal forecasts entirely the wrong way. What's going on? Come learn how meteorologists actually make their weather and climate forecasts, and what it really means when we say there's a 30% chance of rain.

Tom Di Liberto is a climate scientist and award-winning science communicator working as a federal contractor with Groundswell at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Program Office as the senior climate scientist for NOAA’s Climate.gov and social media editor for the NOAA Climate accounts on Twitter, Facebook and Instagram. He has also served as emcee of the Department of State’s U.S. Center at the United Nations climate change conferences COP21, COP22, COP26 and COP27 where he helped lead the U.S. government’s public outreach space during the negotiations.

Questions for Tom may be typed into the chat window during the presentation.

snippet.title: How Early Humans Aligned Their World to the Winter Solstice | The Ancient Science of Light and Stone
snippet.description:
For almost 40,000 years, humans have watched the same moment in the sky: the day the sun stops moving. Long before myths, long before temples, long before the first carved symbols of belief, our ancestors learned to track the winter solstice using nothing but horizons, shadows, mountains, and memory. In this quiet documentary, we explore how early humans across Ice Age Europe, Southwest Asia, the Americas, and the world recognized the solstice as the first predictable astronomical event - and how that recognition slowly shaped measurement, architecture, landscape planning, and the earliest forms of scientific thinking.

On August 24, 79 AD, the people of Pompeii woke up to what seemed like an ordinary Tuesday morning. By sunset, their city would be buried under volcanic ash. This is the story of that last morning.

Follow a single day in ancient Pompeii: the bakers lighting their ovens before dawn, children playing in the streets, merchants opening their shops, families gathering for meals. Experience the normalcy bias that kept most residents from fleeing, the warning signs that went unheeded, and the final hours of one of history's most perfectly preserved cities.

Based on archaeological evidence, historical accounts from Pliny the Younger, and decades of excavation findings, this reconstruction shows what daily life actually looked like in a Roman city and what it means that we can still walk those same streets today.

In the 1950s, Spain under Francisco Franco entered a new phase known as the “Leaden Age.” After years of international isolation following World War II in 1945, the regime began to regain legitimacy. Behind this controlled progress, Franco’s dictatorship remained firmly in place. This period reveals how international recognition and economic change helped secure the long-term survival of one of Europe’s most enduring authoritarian regimes.

snippet.title: The ENTIRE Story of the Japanese Empire – Full Detailed Documentary

We follow Japan from Tokugawa isolation and selective engagement, through the Meiji transformation, constitutional statecraft, and dizzying industrial growth. Watch the empire’s expansion across Korea, Manchuria, and China, the victories against Qing and Russian forces, and the rapid early advances of the Pacific War. 

Then come the reversals: carrier battles, submarine blockades, firebombed cities, and the shattering end that brought surrender and Allied occupation. The story continues into peace, as land reform, a new constitution, rebuilding, and strategic alliances reshape Japan into a technological and cultural power. 

Along the way we connect decisions to consequences—how policy, industry, and ideology created momentum, crisis, and renewal. Clear narration, human moments, and careful sources keep the focus on causality, not spectacle. Whether you are a student or a lifelong learner, this film offers a structured, balanced overview of how Japan moved from isolation to empire, from catastrophe to recovery, and how those legacies still shape the region and the world today.

snippet.title: How the Vikings Lost Every Kingdom They Conquered: The Rise and Fall of the Viking Kings
snippet.description:
They conquered England, governed France, built a kingdom in Sicily, founded the dynasty that became Russia, and served as the personal bodyguard of the Byzantine Emperor in Constantinople. The Norse did not just raid medieval Europe. They ruled it.
And then, within four hundred years, every single one of those positions was gone. No army drove them from England. No uprising expelled them from Sicily. No rival people took Russia back from the dynasty they had founded. This is the viking history documentary that asks the question no standard treatment of the nordic kings ever quite answers: how did the most successful conquerors in medieval European history lose everything they built, without ever being defeated?
The history of the vikings does not end with the raids. It ends with empty thrones, failed dynasties, and the slow disappearance of a people so completely absorbed into the world they had conquered that history forgot to call them conquerors. This is that story.

snippet.title: The Black Death: The City That Forgot How to Mourn
snippet.description:
In the spring of 1348, the Black Death reached Florence — the richest, proudest city in Italy, a place that buried its dead with candles, processions, and a whole street stopping to honour one of its own. Within four months, more than half the city was gone, tipped into pits in the dark without a name or a tear. This is the story of the city that forgot how to mourn.
You live that year through the eyes of one ordinary man: a notary near the old market, whose trade was to write down the names of the dying. He kept his distance, and so he survived. And he watched the city lose something deeper than its dead — its ability to grieve them at all.
The Black Death took the bodies. But first, it took the funerals. This is the account of how grief itself became the plague's first casualty — and the long years in which a city learned, painfully, how to feel again.

localized.description:
In the spring of 1348, the Black Death reached Florence — the richest, proudest city in Italy, a place that buried its dead with candles, processions, and a whole street stopping to honour one of its own. Within four months, more than half the city was gone, tipped into pits in the dark without a name or a tear. This is the story of the city that forgot how to mourn.
You live that year through the eyes of one ordinary man: a notary near the old market, whose trade was to write down the names of the dying. He kept his distance, and so he survived. And he watched the city lose something deeper than its dead — its ability to grieve them at all.
The Black Death took the bodies. But first, it took the funerals. This is the account of how grief itself became the plague's first casualty — and the long years in which a city learned, painfully, how to feel again.

snippet.title: Inside Angkor Wat: The Greatest Temple Complex Ever Built | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Hidden deep within the jungles of Cambodia stands Angkor Wat, the largest religious structure ever built and one of the greatest engineering achievements of the ancient world. Constructed during the height of the Khmer Empire in the 12th century, this vast temple complex covers more than 160 hectares and was completed in just a few decades. But how was such an enormous monument built in the middle of the jungle, and what secrets still remain hidden beneath the landscape surrounding it?

Using cutting-edge technology including satellite mapping, aerial LiDAR scans, and molecular archaeology, researchers are uncovering the lost city that once surrounded Angkor Wat and revealing the sophisticated water systems that sustained one of the world’s largest pre-industrial urban centers. This documentary explores the rise of the Khmer Empire, the spiritual meaning behind the temple’s design, and the mysteries surrounding the decline of this legendary civilization.

snippet.title: The Bronze Age Civilization That Survived the Collapse
snippet.description:
Around twelve hundred BC, the Bronze Age collapsed. The great civilizations of the ancient world fell one after another within a single lifetime, in what may be the first systemic collapse in history. But far to the north, beyond the edge of every map the literate world had ever drawn, one golden world did not fall. It survived for five hundred more years, the last Bronze Age civilization on Earth, buried under more gold than the entire Viking Age would ever produce.
This is the story of the golden kings of the north, a people with no cities and no writing who wired their cold homeland into a trade network spanning a continent, sending amber south to the tombs of pharaohs and drawing bronze and gold back up the long road in return. It is the story of how connection made them rich, how it carried them through a catastrophe that ended the age everywhere else, and how, in the end, a humbler metal that needed no roads quietly brought their golden world to a close.
A long, calm, deeply researched history documentary made for relaxation and sleep. Settle in, dim the lights, and let the story carry you off into the quiet of the night.

snippet.title: Kim Carson | Inspired by Intelligence: Purpose and Creativity in the AI Era | Long Now Talks
snippet.description:
What if AI is not here actually to replace us, but to remind us who we actually are?

That was the question at the heart of Kim Carson’s Long Now Talk. In “Inspired by Intelligence: Purpose and Creativity in the AI Era,” Carson, a creative technologist and futurist, challenged us to avoid the easy narratives of tech-driven utopia and dystopia, charting a course through those two extremes that made the case for AI not as a way to make humans unnecessary but to emphasize our most important creative capacities.

For Carson, AI is a sort of tool for thought — a mirror that we can use to re-inspire ourselves towards greater creativity. Accompanied by video art made using the SORA text-to-video model by Charles Lindsay, she made the case that AI could be used not just for automating labor but also for reclaiming human agency. That means using these new technological modes as enablers for human thought and action, while recognizing their gaps, too — the questions about ourselves that only we can answer, no matter how sophisticated our technology becomes. 

Throughout her talk, Carson expounded upon the power of vulnerability. The ability to use AI tools to help us reconnect with ourselves, to jar us into seeing our own identities and creative capacities in new lights, is one that will fundamentally help us change our world. In Carson’s view, vulnerability and creativity are the necessary precursors to any sort of technological innovation. 

As she ended her remarks, Kim made one final note on how we can make a better world collaboratively and creatively: our society does not need “more optimization, it needs more imagination.”

Carson's new book "Inspired by Intelligence: From Burnout to Becoming" is available starting May 1, 02026: https://shorturl.at/lZnaP

This talk was presented April 22, 02025 at The Interval at Long Now in San Francisco. 
Episode notes: https://longnow.org/ideas/inspired-by-intelligence-purpose-and-creativity-in-the-ai-era/
    
This talk is part of Long Now Talks.

Launched by Stewart Brand in 02003, Long Now Talks has invited more than 400 leading thinkers to share their civilization-scale ideas with a live audience and millions around the globe tuning in to our podcast and videos. Long Now Talks are brought to you by The Long Now Foundation, which has spent the last 25 years igniting cultural imagination around long-term thinking.

By inspiring thought and conversation about how we've been shaped by the last 10,000 years and what might be in store for us over the next 10,000 years, Long Now Talks seek to expand our collective sense of the present moment. Long Now Talks cover futurism and speculative fiction; time, nature, and contemplative practices; the intersection of the humanities and sciences; the evolution of counterculture to cyberculture; cultural imagination, land art and public monuments; and of course, long-term thinking and being a good ancestor.

In our age of compounding crises, The Long Now Foundation is a counterweight — our community of 12,000 strong across 65 countries over our first quarter century. We are a force that imagines new possibilities, thinks critically, and takes action over the long term. We believe that when we all come together, bound by commitment and curiosity, audacious things become possible. Will you join us?  https://longnow.org/join

In 2022, thirty million people watched a monster named Vecna wake up.
The name is older than Stranger Things. The fear is older than the name.

When the Duffer Brothers introduced Vecna in Stranger Things Season 4, they borrowed a name from a 1976 Dungeons & Dragons supplement. But the game designer who created Vecna didn't invent the lich. He inherited it.

This documentary traces the undead wizard back to its oldest roots. We begin with Koshchei the Deathless. The Russian folklore villain who hides his death in a needle, inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, buried on an island no one can find. We witness Odysseus digging a blood pit to summon the dead in Homer's Odyssey. We read the Witch of Endor summoning the prophet Samuel for King Saul.

Then we enter the medieval world of forbidden grimoires: the Munich Manual of Demonic Magic, copied by priests who believed they could command demons in God's name. We follow the Inquisition's crackdown and witness the trial of Gilles de Rais, companion of Joan of Arc, executed for invoking the demon Barron.

The Hand of Glory: a mummified criminal's hand that could freeze households  becomes the template for D&D's Hand of Vecna. The Black Death's corpse phenomena create the revenant myths that haunt European folklore. And Terror Management Theory reveals why we keep telling the same story: there is a way to cheat death, and the price is your humanity.

snippet.description:
Beneath the streets of London, buried inside Alpine mountains, sunk into the plains of occupied Poland, and hidden along the Atlantic coast of France, some of the most extraordinary structures of the Second World War were built in secret and never fully seen by the public. Churchill directed the war from a bunker disguised as a government basement, with a hotline to Roosevelt hidden behind a door marked "toilet." Mussolini built a 1,500-kilometre wall of Alpine fortresses partly to defend against his own ally, Hitler, while secretly storing 127 tons of Italy's national gold inside. Nazi Germany constructed a bunker line 30 metres underground that stretched over 100 kilometres along the Polish border in direct violation of Versailles. And in Lorient, France, concrete pens so thick that Allied bombing campaigns lasting four years left them completely intact while destroying 75% of the city around them. These are the bunkers that concrete built and history forgot.

snippet.description:

Before Eve, there was Lilith, and she refused to submit.
This is the 5,000-year true story of the demon queen who became a feminist icon.

In 1997, Sarah McLachlan named her all-female music festival after a demon. The Lilith Fair became the highest-grossing touring festival of that summer, raising seven million dollars for women's charities. The name came from medieval Jewish legend: Adam's first wife, who demanded equality and flew from Eden rather than lie beneath her husband.

But Lilith's story begins three thousand years before that concert stage. In the wind-swept ziggurats of ancient Babylon, families buried clay bowls beneath their thresholds, traps for malevolent spirits, with a wild-haired demon drawn at the center. Her name was Lilith. And she was coming for the children.

This documentary traces Lilith through five millennia of human fear and desire. We examine the archaeological evidence of incantation bowls and protective amulets. We explore the medieval texts that turned a nameless demon into Adam's rebellious first wife. We witness her coronation as queen of darkness in Kabbalah, her transformation into Victorian femme fatale, and her stunning reclamation by feminist theologians who saw in her ancient defiance a message for modern women.

No figure in mythology has been more completely transformed. She has been screech owl and night hag, seductress and child-thief, cosmic evil and feminist inspiration. Tonight, we discover why.

snippet.title: The Copper Age | The Forgotten Age Between Stone and Bronze | History for Sleep
snippet.description:
The Copper Age was the forgotten age between the Stone Age and the Bronze Age, when human beings first learned to draw metal from the earth. Also known as the Chalcolithic Age, the age of copper and stone together, it was the quiet hinge on which the whole metal world turned. This long, calm history documentary for sleep follows that forgotten age from the first gleam of copper to the coming of bronze, told gently to help you drift off.
These history stories for sleep are made for rest. Let the quiet narration carry you through the dawn of metal: the settled villages of the first farmers, the discovery of the bright stone, the smith and his secret craft, the shining trade that connected the ancient world, the gold of Varna and the birth of inequality, and the long road that led on toward the Bronze Age.
Whether you are here to fall asleep to the story of the first metalworkers, to relax to the history of the Copper Age, or simply to rest a while in a quieter, older world, this slow history is made to serve that. There is nothing to do now but listen, and let the long story carry you down into sleep.
History for Sleep creates long, relaxing history documentaries and sleep stories for adults, built from real history and told gently to help you fall asleep. Calm narration, no sudden sounds, and the deep human story carried softly into rest.
